title: Discerning and Resolving Knowledge Conflicts through Adaptive Decoding with Contextual Information-Entropy Constraint
artifacts_released: Y - code at https://github.com/Stacy027/COIECD
models_evaluated: LLaMA2-7B; LLaMA2-13B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; FLAN-T5-3B; FLAN-T5-11B; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (appendix comparison only)
datasets_benchmarks: NaturalQuestions; SQuAD 1.1; StrategyQA (each split post-hoc into conflicting vs non-conflicting subsets rather than synthetically perturbed); Counterfacts (Longpre et al. 2021, fully synthetic conflicts)
key_result: COIECD improves over regular decoding on every realistic dataset while prior conflict-resolution decoders degrade on non-conflicting data: on NQ it gains EM +0.94/F1 +1.38 (LLaMA2-13B), +10.33 EM/+14.52 F1 (OPT-6.7B) and +2.84 EM/+1.67 F1 (FLAN-T5-3B), where contrastive decoding and context-aware decoding lose 8.38 and 7.09 EM respectively on FLAN-T5-3B. The claimed contribution is robustness across the conflict/non-conflict mix, not peak counterfactual accuracy.
baselines_compared: Regular (greedy) decoding; Self-Consistency (Wang et al. 2023b, 40 samples); Contrastive Decoding (Li et al. 2023b); Context-Aware Decoding (Shi et al. 2023a). All baselines reproduced by the authors rather than quoted.
threat_model: N/A - no adversary. The paper treats knowledge conflict as an incidental property of real retrieval corpora, where retrieved context legitimately contradicts stale parametric knowledge, and explicitly criticizes prior work for only studying synthetically constructed conflicts.
stated_limitations: Authors state they evaluate only on QA and not on other context-intensive tasks such as summarization; that like CD and CAD the method costs roughly double regular decoding because two decoding passes are required; and that they omit entropy smoothing in the constraint, which is acceptable for short QA answers but is flagged as a limitation for open-ended generation.
technical_summary: Proposes COIECD, an adaptive decoding rule that first discerns whether a knowledge conflict is actually present before intervening. Frames the token-level decision via an information-entropy constraint: tokens whose contextual information content falls outside a stable-entropy band are treated as conflict points and decoded with a context-favoring objective, while non-conflict tokens fall through to regular decoding. Evaluates on NQ, SQuAD, StrategyQA and Counterfacts across LLaMA2, OPT and FLAN-T5 against Regular, SC, CD and CAD. Shows the central empirical point that existing conflict-solving decoders buy faithfulness on conflicting context at a real accuracy cost on non-conflicting context, which the adaptive gate avoids.

title: A Critical Evaluation of Defenses against Prompt Injection Attacks: [Dataset/Tool Paper]
artifacts_released: Y - code and data at https://github.com/PIEval123/PIEval, including the new MMLU-PI benchmark
models_evaluated: Llama-3-8B-Instruct (undefended reference); Llama-3-8B-Instruct-StruQ; Llama-3-8B-Instruct-SecAlign; GPT-4o-mini (as the deployed Instruction Hierarchy system); PromptGuard and Attention Tracker detector checkpoints; Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct
datasets_benchmarks: OpenPromptInjection (Liu et al. USENIX Sec 2024), 4,900 prompt-response pairs; MMLU-PI, a new prompt-injection benchmark the authors construct from MMLU; AlpacaFarm referenced as the inadequate utility benchmark used by prior work
key_result: Re-evaluating released defense artifacts under a principled protocol overturns their published claims: StruQ and SecAlign lose real general-purpose utility (0.11/0.10 and 0.17/0.11 drops vs Llama-3-8B-Instruct on the two benchmarks), GCG-optimized injection reaches ASV above 0.80 against StruQ on both benchmarks and 0.72 against SecAlign on MMLU-PI, and GPT-4o-mini with Instruction Hierarchy falls to the plain existing Combined Attack at ASV 0.68 and 0.75. Detectors look strong by AUC but fail in deployment terms, with Attention Tracker at 0.69 FNR on MMLU-PI and the authors' adaptive separator attack driving evasion to 0.66 and 1.00.
baselines_compared: The defenses themselves are the objects of comparison, each run from its released artifact against an undefended Llama-3-8B-Instruct reference: StruQ, SecAlign, Instruction Hierarchy (via GPT-4o-mini), PromptGuard and Attention Tracker. Attacks compared are Naive, Escape-Characters, Context-Ignoring, Fake-Completion, Combined, GCG-optimized, and the authors' adaptive framework.
threat_model: The attacker controls the data segment of the prompt, which reaches the LLM from an untrusted source such as a web page, a product review or a tool description, and embeds an injected prompt to substitute an attacker-chosen task for the intended one. The paper's central methodological claim is that the adaptive attacker must also be assumed to know the defense and optimize against it, which prior evaluations omitted.
stated_limitations: Authors limit GCG-based optimization to the separator (and in one ablation the injected instruction) for computational reasons rather than optimizing the full contaminated sample, so the reported adaptive ASVs are lower bounds. They frame the work as a foundation for evaluating future defenses rather than a defense of their own, and note that a defense's utility conclusions depend on which general-purpose benchmark is chosen.
technical_summary: Evaluates recent prompt injection defenses under a two-dimensional protocol the authors argue prior work lacked: effectiveness against both existing and adaptive attacks across diverse target and injected prompts, and general-purpose utility measured in absolute terms on large benchmarks rather than relative to an equally weak fine-tuned control. Runs the released StruQ, SecAlign, PromptGuard and Attention Tracker artifacts plus deployed GPT-4o-mini Instruction Hierarchy, and introduces MMLU-PI alongside OpenPromptInjection. Proposes a general adaptive attack framework that optimizes a separator string to jointly induce the attacker-desired response and evade detection. Concludes that every defense examined is materially weaker than its own paper reported, and that AUC-only detector reporting hides deployment-relevant FPR/FNR failures.

title: AttackEval: How to Evaluate the Effectiveness of Jailbreak Attacking on Large Language Models
artifacts_released: N - a ground-truth dataset is described as a contribution but no repository or download link appears in the text
models_evaluated: GPT-3.5-Turbo; GPT-4; LLaMA2-7B; LLaMA3-8B; Gemma-7B; ChatGLM-6B. GPT-4 additionally serves as the judge model for the metric itself.
datasets_benchmarks: jailbreak_llms collection (666 jailbreak prompts compiled from forums, websites and open-source sets; 390 harmful questions spanning 13 forbidden scenarios); the authors curate a ground-truth answer set over these questions as their own benchmark contribution
key_result: The proposed 0-1 graded metric tracks the binary ASR baseline in aggregate ranking (Political Lobbying is the highest-effectiveness scenario under both) but consistently assigns non-zero effectiveness to a slice of prompts that binary ASR scores as complete failures, so it classifies a slightly higher share of prompts as harmful. Per-scenario coarse-grained means run roughly 0.33-0.65 against baseline values of 0.30-0.63, with the second- and third-ranked scenarios swapping order between the two metrics.
baselines_compared: Binary Attack Success Rate (ASR) as used in prior jailbreak work, computed over the same models and prompts; the comparison is agreement/divergence between the graded metric and ASR rather than a competing method.
threat_model: The attacker submits jailbreak prompts directly to the model to elicit content the safety training forbids, using role-play, scenario framing or obfuscated phrasing. No indirect or third-party content channel is assumed, and the attacker needs only black-box query access.
stated_limitations: The paper has no limitations section. It concedes in passing that evaluation methods relying on LLM judges 'may not be trustworthy' and that its own fine-grained variant still depends on GPT-4 as judge unless ground truth is supplied, but it does not enumerate limitations of its own framework.
technical_summary: Proposes AttackEval, a pair of evaluation frameworks that score jailbreak prompt effectiveness on a continuous 0-1 scale instead of the conventional binary success/failure. The coarse-grained variant aggregates weighted scores across an ensemble of target LLMs to rate a prompt against an integrated multi-model system; the fine-grained variant scores a single response, either against curated ground truth or via a GPT-4 judge. Builds a ground-truth answer set over 390 harmful questions and 666 jailbreak prompts drawn from an existing collection. Validates chiefly by showing rank agreement with binary ASR while surfacing partially-effective prompts that ASR discards as harmless; it proposes no attack and no defense.

title: Ranking Manipulation for Conversational Search Engines
artifacts_released: Y - data collection and experiment source code released; the RAGDOLL dataset released as product page URLs under CC-BY-4.0
models_evaluated: GPT-3.5 Turbo; GPT-4 Turbo; Llama 3 70B; perplexity.ai Sonar Large Online (as a surrogate for the production perplexity.ai search tool, with anecdotal checks against the full tool); mxbai-embed-large for document embedding analysis
datasets_benchmarks: RAGDOLL, a new dataset of real consumer product websites the authors collect via an automated LLM-plus-search pipeline over Common Crawl: 5 product groups x 10 categories (50 categories), with 8 brands per category used in the main experiments
key_result: A tree-of-attacks jailbreaking procedure reliably promotes arbitrary low-ranked products in conversational search output, and the injections transfer from GPT-4 Turbo templates to a production system: against perplexity.ai's Sonar Large Online, with the adversarial page self-hosted and the injection interspersed 15 times through the HTML, promoted products gain almost 3 ranking positions on average and close more than half the gap to the top rank. Separately, the un-attacked analysis shows LLMs differ sharply in what drives ranking, with GPT-4 Turbo weighting the product name heavily and being minimally influenced by retrieved document content.
baselines_compared: Natural (un-injected) ranking distributions serve as the control, measured per model and per product category; the authors also compare across GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4 Turbo and Llama 3 70B and across white-box context injection versus black-box hosted-webpage delivery. No competing attack method is compared.
threat_model: A website owner with a financial incentive to be recommended controls the content of their own product page, which a conversational search engine scrapes and loads into the LLM context. The initial analysis assumes the attacker can set the extracted text directly; this is then relaxed to a fully black-box setting where the attacker only hosts a page at a neutral URL and the production engine does its own scraping and chunking, with the injected text hideable by standard SEO techniques.
stated_limitations: Authors state the attack is not completely effective, though most promoted products improve substantially; that cost constraints forced a shallow tree-of-attacks search with only m=2 evaluation responses, so a well-resourced attacker would do better; and, notably, that they do not evaluate any of the existing partially-effective defenses against their attack.
technical_summary: Formalizes conversational search ranking as an adversarial problem and shows that prompt injection into retrieved web content reorders the sources an LLM search engine recommends. Introduces RAGDOLL, a controlled dataset of real consumer product pages, and first disentangles the natural ranking influence of product name, document content and context position, finding these weights differ markedly between LLMs. Then applies a tree-of-attacks-style jailbreak search to craft page-embedded injections that promote a chosen product. Demonstrates end-to-end black-box transfer by hosting manipulated pages and having perplexity.ai's Sonar Large Online scrape them, gaining roughly 3 ranking positions; proposes no defense and explicitly declines to test existing ones.

title: A Study on Prompt Injection Attack Against LLM-Integrated Mobile Robotic Systems
artifacts_released: N - no repository, code link or data release mentioned anywhere in the text
models_evaluated: GPT-4o only, as the controller of a simulated mobile robot in the EyeSim VR simulator
datasets_benchmarks: None - no public benchmark. The authors run their own simulated mission-oriented navigation scenarios in EyeSim VR with multi-modal input (camera image, LiDAR scan, human instruction), sweeping injected-attack rates of 0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 1.0.
key_result: Secure prompting with a reasoning-first response format yields a headline 30.8% general improvement (overall attack detection improvement plus 24.4% overall performance improvement). The sharpest finding is that Goal Hijacking Injection is completely undetectable without the defense (precision, recall and F1 all exactly zero), while with the defense precision rises to 0.9-1.0 but recall reaches only 0.13-0.54; mission performance (MOER) under OMI attack recovers from a 0.5-to-0.13 decline to a peak of 0.67. Costs are a 23.9% weighted response-time increase and 2.9% more tokens.
baselines_compared: Only an internal no-defence control of the same GPT-4o robot system at matched attack rates. No competing defense and no competing attack method is compared, although the related-work section discusses Navigational Prompt Engineering (Wen et al.) without evaluating it.
threat_model: Assumes an end-to-end LLM-controlled robot where multi-modal sensory data feeds directly into the LLM and the LLM's output directly drives motion. The attacker injects malicious prompts through compromised sensor data or adversarial instructions (for example tampering with the camera feed to replace an obstacle with clear path, or issuing a plausible-sounding instruction that contradicts the mission objective), aiming to cause collisions or mission failure rather than to extract data.
stated_limitations: Authors state the 28.1% weighted recall improvement means false negatives remain, so sophisticated attacks can still bypass the defense; that the added token usage and 23.9% response-time overhead may be unsustainable for real-time or resource-constrained robots; and that EyeSim VR does not replicate real-world complexity, so a sim2real gap should be expected and real trials are needed.
technical_summary: Evaluates prompt injection against a GPT-4o-controlled mobile robot whose navigation decisions come directly from multi-modal sensory prompts. Defines two injection classes the authors name Obvious Malicious Injection, which contradicts common sense, and Goal Hijacking Injection, which reads as a plausible navigation instruction while contradicting the mission objective, plus a control-signal variant the LLM cannot identify at all. Applies a secure prompting mitigation that forces the LLM to reason over each modality in natural language and then emit a per-modality attack verdict in a structured response format. Measures detection precision/recall/F1 and a mission-oriented efficiency rate across sweeping attack rates in the EyeSim VR simulator, reporting a 30.8% aggregate improvement under a bespoke weighted metric.

title: PromptLocate: Localizing Prompt Injection Attacks
artifacts_released: Y - code and data at https://github.com/liu00222/Open-Prompt-Injection
models_evaluated: LLaMA3-8B-Instruct as the backend LLM targeted by optimization-based attacks; GPT-4o as the backend on AgentDojo; three further backend LLMs in an appendix table; DataSentinel (fine-tuned) reused as the segment-level detection oracle
datasets_benchmarks: OpenPromptInjection (seven target tasks, results averaged over all 7x7 target-injected task combinations); AgentDojo (Banking, Travel, Workspace, Slack environments, injections embedded in tool-call output); TaskTracker (1,000 training / 500 test samples); JailbreakBench (100 prompts per attack type inserted into 100 clean samples); a 556-sample validation set the authors construct for threshold selection
key_result: PromptLocate reaches 0.93-0.99 localization (RL) and ES scores with 0.95-1.00 precision and recall across all attack settings on OpenPromptInjection, and above 0.95 on AgentDojo Banking and above 0.85 on Travel and Workspace, with attack success after removal dropping sharply even where recall is lower. The striking robustness result is that its DataSentinel-based oracle still misses 63% of contaminated segments at segment level (81% untailored), yet the segment-group search and contextual-inconsistency step recover accurate localization anyway. Two competing approaches score only 0.53/0.53 and 0.76/0.72 RL/ES on the same Combined Attack; runtime is about 11 seconds per contaminated sample on an RTX A5000.
baselines_compared: Three feature-attribution localizers adapted to this task - Single Feature Attribution (SFA), Feature Removal Attribution (FRA) and Shapley Value Attribution (SVA) - each also in a threshold-tuned variant (SFA-T, FRA-T, SVA-T) using the same validation set. A concurrent segment-classification method and Abdelnabi et al.'s distance-to-primary detector are additionally adapted for localization and compared. Baselines are inapplicable on AgentDojo because they need full output probabilities, which GPT-4o does not expose.
threat_model: The attacker contaminates data reaching the LLM from an untrusted source (web pages, product reviews, or tool-call results in the agent setting) with an injected prompt containing both injected instructions and injected data. The defender is assumed to run post-detection forensics: localization is applied only to samples already flagged as contaminated, and the defender does not know which attack was used. Eight adaptive attacks are constructed against the localizer itself, including one (Period) that inserts random periods to break segmentation.
stated_limitations: Authors note that where data has a natural segmentation (one review per user) Step I can be skipped, but Steps II and III remain necessary because an attacker can split an injected prompt across several natural segments. They list stronger adaptive prompt injection attacks and localization methods with provable security guarantees as open problems, implying the present guarantees are purely empirical.
technical_summary: Proposes PromptLocate, the first method for localizing an injected prompt inside contaminated data rather than merely detecting that contamination occurred, motivated by post-attack forensics and clean-data recovery. Splits contaminated data into semantically coherent segments using a threshold tuned on a validation set, then identifies instruction-contaminated segments with a segment-group-based search over a detector repurposed as an oracle, and finally pinpoints data-contaminated segments via contextual inconsistency without needing the oracle. Evaluates across eight existing and eight adaptive attacks on OpenPromptInjection and AgentDojo, plus TaskTracker and JailbreakBench transfers. Shows the method tolerates a substantially unreliable oracle and that removing the localized span neutralizes the attack.

title: Preemptive Answer "Attacks" on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
artifacts_released: N - no code or data link appears in the text
models_evaluated: ChatGPT (gpt-3.5 via the OpenAI chat API) and GPT-4
datasets_benchmarks: Six reasoning datasets, 500 randomly sampled test items each: GSM8K, MathQA, MATH, HotpotQA, CommonsenseQA and StrategyQA. Three CoT regimes are crossed with these: Zero-Shot CoT, Few-Shot CoT and each with Self-Consistency.
key_result: Committing to an answer before reasoning measurably degrades CoT accuracy across nearly all dataset/model/CoT combinations: on GSM8K with ChatGPT, accuracy falls from 74.4 to 63.0 (unintentional) and 68.2 (malicious) under Zero-Shot CoT, and from 76.8 to 57.3 and 71.1 under Few-Shot CoT. Notably the unintentional variant is as harmful as the malicious one on the three arithmetic datasets, GPT-4 is more robust than ChatGPT, few-shot ICL provides no protection over zero-shot, and self-consistency helps but does not eliminate the loss. The two mitigations consistently lower ASR and raise accuracy but never fully negate the effect.
baselines_compared: A no-preemptive-answer control ('N') for every model/dataset/CoT cell, plus cross-comparison of Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot CoT and with/without Self-Consistency. The two mitigations are compared against the unmitigated attacked condition. BadChain is discussed as a stronger dedicated attack but is not run.
threat_model: Two variants are studied side by side. In the unintentional case there is no attacker at all: the user's own prompt phrasing ('first give an answer, then show the step-by-step solution') causes the model to emit an answer before reasoning. In the malicious case a user performs prompt injection to force the same answer-first ordering with an attacker-chosen answer. The attacker needs only prompt-level access and no model internals.
stated_limitations: Authors state they deliberately do not craft optimized attack techniques, so their ASR is not comparable with dedicated attack papers such as BadChain; that they study only answer-first scenarios and omit cases where the answer is scrutinized before being given, which limits real-world coverage; and that their exploration of mitigation is shallow, with simplicity and breadth offered as the compensating advantage.
technical_summary: Introduces the preemptive answer scenario, in which an LLM produces an answer before it reasons, and shows that the subsequent chain-of-thought degrades to rationalizing that answer rather than deriving one. Distinguishes an unintentional variant arising from ordinary answer-first prompt phrasing from a malicious variant induced by prompt injection, and measures both with accuracy and an attack success rate across six reasoning datasets, two models and three CoT methods. Finds the incidental and adversarial variants inflict comparable damage on arithmetic tasks, which makes this one of the few papers in the corpus to instrument both failure modes under one protocol. Proposes two lightweight mitigations, problem restatement and self-reflection, which reduce but do not remove the degradation.

title: EchoLeak: The First Real-World Zero-Click Prompt Injection Exploit in a Production LLM System
artifacts_released: N - nothing released; an open-source Copilot-like sandbox for reproducing EchoLeak is listed only as future work
models_evaluated: None - no model was run. The subject is Microsoft 365 Copilot as a production system, analyzed from public disclosure material rather than measured.
datasets_benchmarks: None - no dataset or benchmark. The paper is a single-incident case study of CVE-2025-32711 built from Aim Labs' public disclosure, NVD entries and vendor documentation.
key_result: Documents that a single crafted email achieved zero-click exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot by chaining four independent bypasses: evading Microsoft's XPIA cross-prompt-injection classifier, defeating link redaction via reference-style Markdown, triggering auto-fetched images so no click is needed, and routing the outbound request through a Microsoft Teams proxy that the Content Security Policy already allowed. The analytical claim is that each layer failed for an independent reason, so defense-in-depth composed of single-point filters does not hold; the supporting defense-to-attack-step mapping is explicitly labelled theoretical.
baselines_compared: None - no experimental comparison. Table 3 offers a theoretical mapping of candidate mitigations against each step of the attack chain, with no measurement behind the success/failure marks.
threat_model: An external adversary with no insider access and no ability to query Copilot directly, who can only send an ordinary-looking email (no malware, no attachment) to an employee of the target organization. The victim has Copilot enabled with read access to their own mail and files, and merely needs to invoke Copilot at some later point for an unrelated purpose. Existing protections assumed present are the XPIA input classifier, output link redaction and browser CSP.
stated_limitations: Authors state plainly that the work rests solely on already-public data and that they did not reproduce the attack or run any experiments, so conclusions about proprietary filters are inferential and the reproduction discussion refers to a conceptual analog rather than production Copilot. They further note they did not practically evaluate the mitigations they propose, that some are reportedly already deployed which limits comparability, that scope was restricted to indirect prompt injection, and that the analysis was done roughly two months post-disclosure.
technical_summary: Analyzes EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711), the first publicly confirmed zero-click prompt injection to cause real data exfiltration from a production LLM assistant. Reconstructs the full kill chain from the attacker's email through Copilot's retrieval of that email, the encoding of sensitive context into a reference-style Markdown image URL, and the browser's automatic fetch of that URL through a CSP-permitted Microsoft domain. Explains why each deployed defense layer failed independently and proposes engineering mitigations spanning prompt scope isolation, input/output filtering, provenance-based access control and strict egress-constraining CSP. Runs no experiments, reproduces nothing and evaluates no mitigation, so its value to the corpus is as a documented real-world incident and threat-model reference rather than as evidence.

title: Detecting LLM-generated peer reviews
artifacts_released: Y - all code and result files stated to be in a public repository
models_evaluated: ChatGPT 4o; o1-mini; Gemini 2.0 Flash; Claude 3.5 Sonnet; LLaMA 2; Vicuna 1.5 (the last two used for GCG-optimized cryptic prompts on A100/H100 GPUs)
datasets_benchmarks: ICLR 2024 submissions (100 via API, 30 for manual upload); International Congress on Peer Review and Scientific Publication (PRC) 2022 abstracts; PeerRead; 52 NSF grant proposals from Open Grants; for the false-positive analysis, real review corpora including 28,028 ICLR 2024 reviews and a pre-ChatGPT-era ICLR 2021 set
key_result: Inserting a randomly generated fake citation as the watermark succeeds in 98.6% of LLM-generated reviews on average across models and injection techniques, and 89% on NSF grant proposals; GCG-optimized cryptic prompts reach 91% and hit 19 of 20 samples. The watermark survives the obvious reviewer countermeasure, with over 94% retention after paraphrasing by a second LLM. The FWER-controlling hypothesis tests keep high power with zero false positives across more than ten thousand real reviews, while Bonferroni and Holm-Bonferroni corrections are too conservative to be usable at that scale.
baselines_compared: Bonferroni and Holm-Bonferroni multiple-testing corrections as the statistical baselines for the detection test; GPTZero-style LLM-text detectors are cited as the inadequate prior approach but are not re-run. Three injection strategies (white-text font embedding, tiny font, GCG-optimized cryptic prompts) are compared against each other, and three reviewer defense strategies including paraphrasing are used as the adversarial control.
threat_model: Inverted relative to the rest of the corpus: the party doing the injecting is the defender (the venue or organizers, who control the manuscript PDF), and the adversary is a disengaged reviewer who violates policy by uploading the manuscript to an LLM and submitting its output. The reviewer may attempt evasion by paraphrasing, stripping hidden text, or instructing the LLM to ignore embedded instructions. The paper separately acknowledges the genuinely malicious case, where a paper author injects prompts to bias an LLM reviewer toward higher ratings, and gives it only a preliminary evaluation.
stated_limitations: Authors frame detection of misuse and evasion of that detection as an ongoing arms race rather than a solved problem, and note the extension to general text generation is future work. They explicitly flag the unaddressed converse risk that authors can use the same indirect prompt injection channel to inflate their own reviews, noting safeguards are needed on both sides.
technical_summary: Repurposes indirect prompt injection as an enforcement mechanism, embedding hidden instructions in a manuscript PDF that cause any LLM reading it to plant a covert watermark, such as a fabricated citation or rare phrase, in the review it generates. Contributes a rigorous watermarking and hypothesis-testing framework that controls family-wise error rate across many reviews with higher power than Bonferroni-style corrections and without assuming anything about human writing style. Compares white-text embedding, tiny-font embedding and GCG-optimized cryptic prompts, and tests resilience against reviewer countermeasures including paraphrasing. Validates on real ICLR, PeerRead, PRC and NSF corpora, and confirms the false-positive bounds empirically on over ten thousand genuine reviews.

title: FATH: Authentication-based Test-time Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
artifacts_released: Y - code at https://github.com/Jayfeather1024/FATH
models_evaluated: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct (1x NVIDIA A100) and gpt-3.5-turbo, both at default generation parameters
datasets_benchmarks: OpenPromptInjection+ , the authors' extension of OpenPromptInjection that swaps the 7 fixed tasks for 100 general Stanford Alpaca instructions per injection task across three injection categories (URL, QA, CLF); and InjecAgent, using all 510 direct-harm text examples
key_result: FATH reaches the lowest ASR of any compared defense on all five Threat Model 1 attacks across three injection tasks and both backbones, driving ASR to near 0% and to exactly 0% against the Combined Attack on InjecAgent. Under Threat Model 2 adaptive attacks, which know the defense in full and are strong enough to beat Combined Attack against every other method, FATH still holds 0% ASR on GPT-3.5 and 0% on InjecAgent, with a reduced but non-zero ASR on Llama3. The cost is a small drop in judge score on benign utility.
baselines_compared: Four established test-time defenses: Instructional Prevention, Sandwich Prevention, Text Instruction Isolation (all Liu et al. 2023b) and In-context Learning Defense (Yi et al. 2023), plus a No Defense control. Attacks compared are Naive, Escape Characters, Context Ignoring, Fake Completion and Combined under Threat Model 1, plus per-defense hand-designed Adaptive Attacks under Threat Model 2.
threat_model: The attacker controls only external text that the application feeds to the LLM (web pages, emails, tool results) and cannot touch the user instruction or the model. Two tiers are specified: Threat Model 1 where the attacker is unaware of the deployed defense, and Threat Model 2 where the attacker knows the defense completely and tailors the injection to it, including a variant that fabricates hash-style boundary tags to try to place its response in the authorized section. Optimization-based attacks are framed as the worst case.
stated_limitations: Authors state FATH needs substantial manual effort to design defense prompts per application, evidenced by how different the templates are between their two benchmarks. They note it depends on strong instruction-following and would likely degrade on weaker models such as Alpaca. They also concede that because no benchmark offers real tool usage, they simulate tool execution results by supplying external text directly.
technical_summary: Proposes FATH, a test-time defense that treats instruction handling as an authentication problem rather than a filtering problem. Generates five HMAC-derived hash tags per request, formats the prompt so user instructions and external text are segregated under input authentication tags, and prompts the LLM with a security policy requiring it to emit each response wrapped in an authorized or unauthorized output tag, aided by chain-of-thought and in-context examples. Enforces the decision outside the model by rule-based parsing of the raw output, extracting only the section carrying the correct unguessable tag, so any response elicited by an injected instruction is discarded. Evaluates on OpenPromptInjection+ and InjecAgent against four prompt-level baseline defenses under both defense-unaware and fully defense-aware adaptive attackers.

rq3.note: No new named attack. The paper constructs per-defense Adaptive Attacks under Threat Model 2, but these are unnamed evaluation instruments built to stress-test its own and the baselines' defenses, not offered as a general attack technique.

rq4.name: FATH (Formatting AuThentication with Hash-based tags)
rq4.note: Named test-time authentication defense with released code. Coded as execution because security comes from rule-based parsing of the raw output to keep only the section carrying an unguessable HMAC tag, though the method also formats input (ingestion) and prompts a security policy (reasoning). Evaluation is purely adversarial (OpenPromptInjection+, InjecAgent); no incidental degradation is tested.

title: Applying Pre-trained Multilingual BERT in Embeddings for Improved Malicious Prompt Injection Attacks Detection
artifacts_released: N - no code, model or data repository is mentioned
models_evaluated: No LLM is attacked or defended. Embedding/classification models only: bert-base-multilingual-uncased and DistilBERT as encoders, with Gaussian Naive Bayes, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine and Logistic Regression as downstream classifiers.
datasets_benchmarks: The deepset Prompt Injection Dataset from HuggingFace: 662 samples total, using the original 546 train / 116 test split, two columns (text, label), mostly English with some translations such as German
key_result: Multilingual BERT embeddings with Logistic Regression reach 96.55% accuracy, 1.00 precision, 0.9333 recall and 0.9655 F1 on the 116-sample holdout, ahead of SVM (0.9568), Random Forest (0.8965) and Gaussian Naive Bayes (0.8879). The headline claim to outperform 'existing works' rests on a table comparing these numbers against published accuracies for unrelated tasks and corpora (Fake or Real News, Weibo, CSE-Persistence), not against any prompt injection detector.
baselines_compared: Internal comparison among the four classical classifiers and between multilingual BERT and DistilBERT embeddings. No prompt injection detection baseline (PromptGuard, perplexity filtering, LLM-as-detector) is run; the external comparison is against accuracies reported for different datasets and different tasks entirely.
threat_model: N/A - essentially absent. The paper asserts that malicious prompt injection threatens real LLM applications but specifies no attacker capability, no injection channel, no adaptivity and no deployment setting. The task is reduced to offline binary classification of a fixed labelled prompt corpus.
stated_limitations: No limitations section. The abstract mentions investigating incorrect predictions 'to gain insights into its limitations', and the Future Works section says only that the authors will fine-tune pre-trained LLMs to improve detection; the small dataset, absent adversarial evaluation and mismatched external comparison are not acknowledged.
technical_summary: Evaluates an off-the-shelf pipeline for flagging malicious prompts: tokenize with multilingual BERT or DistilBERT, take the embeddings, and train Gaussian Naive Bayes, Random Forest, SVM or Logistic Regression as a binary classifier. Uses the 662-sample deepset prompt injection dataset with its stock train/test split and reports accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC/AUC per classifier. Concludes that multilingual BERT embeddings plus Logistic Regression give the best accuracy at 96.55%. Introduces no new architecture, loss, detection principle or dataset, and runs no adversarial or adaptive evaluation.

rq3.note: Proposes no attack or degradation mechanism at all; the paper is purely a detection-classification study.

rq4.note: No named defense. Applies existing pre-trained encoders and textbook classifiers to an existing public dataset; the pipeline is never named or characterized as a distinct contribution, and it is not compared against any actual prompt-injection detector.

title: TopicAttack: An Indirect Prompt Injection Attack via Topic Transition
artifacts_released: Y - code at https://github.com/LukeChen-go/topicattack
models_evaluated: Open-source: Llama3-8B-Instruct, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2-7B-Instruct, Llama3-70B-Instruct, Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, Llama3.1-405B-Instruct, Qwen2-72B-Instruct. Closed-source: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1.
datasets_benchmarks: Inj-SQuAD and Inj-TriviaQA (injected-QA sets derived from SQuAD and TriviaQA with phishing, advertisement and propaganda injected instructions, from Chen et al. 2025b) for the chatbot setting; InjecAgent 'Direct Harm' subset, 510 samples, for the agent setting
key_result: Framing the injection as a gradual conversational topic transition rather than an abrupt instruction break holds up where every baseline attack collapses under defense. Against SecAlign on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, TopicAttack reaches 90.67% and 93.89% ASR on Inj-SQuAD and Inj-TriviaQA while all baselines stay below 10%. On closed-source models it gets 99.78-100% undefended and retains up to 99.00% under Sandwich and 99.56% under Spotlight, against Combined attack's 9.00% under Sandwich on GPT-4o. In agents it takes the best ASR in 8 of 12 large-model configurations and all closed-source configurations. An attention analysis supplies the mechanism: higher injected-to-original attention ratio predicts success, and TopicAttack achieves a much higher ratio than baselines.
baselines_compared: Attack baselines: Naive, Ignore, Escape-Character, Fake completion and Combined, plus GCG and AutoDAN in an optimization-attack comparison. Defense baselines the attack is run against: Sandwich and Spotlight (training-free) and StruQ and SecAlign (fine-tuned), each actually executed rather than cited.
threat_model: The attacker can manipulate only external data content that the LLM later retrieves through a tool such as a search engine, and has no knowledge of the application system, its prompts or its deployed defense. No model access, gradients or query feedback are assumed, which is what makes the reported transfer to GPT-4o and to fine-tuned defenses meaningful.
stated_limitations: Authors state that limited training resources prevented them from fine-tuning models above 70B, so those are evaluated only against prompt-engineering defenses; that the method still requires a hand-designed meta-prompt to make the LLM generate suitable transitions; and that because the approach is prompt engineering they can offer empirical evidence and explanation but no formal proof of effectiveness.
technical_summary: Proposes TopicAttack, an indirect prompt injection method that hides the seam between benign data and the injected instruction. Prompts an LLM to fabricate a short conversational transition passage that starts from a topic related to the host document and drifts step by step toward the attacker's instruction, so the injection never presents the abrupt context break that defenses like Sandwich and Spotlight key on. Adds a reminding prompt designed to hold the model's attention on the injected instruction and pull it off the original one, and validates that mechanism by measuring injected-to-original attention ratios. Evaluates across ten models from 7B to 405B and both chatbot and agent settings, against four deployed defenses including the fine-tuned StruQ and SecAlign.

rq3.name: TopicAttack
rq3.note: Named, distinct injection technique: an LLM-generated gradual topic-transition prefix plus a reminding prompt that redistributes attention toward the injected instruction. Clears the bar easily, with released code and an attention-based mechanistic account.

rq4.note: Attack paper only. It runs Sandwich, Spotlight, StruQ and SecAlign as targets to be defeated and proposes no defense of its own.

title: LLMail-Inject: A Dataset from a Realistic Adaptive Prompt Injection Challenge
artifacts_released: Y - dataset on HuggingFace (microsoft/llmail-inject-challenge, MIT license), challenge code and analysis code both on GitHub
models_evaluated: microsoft/Phi-3-medium-128k-instruct (tool calling emulated by prompting and JSON parsing, since the model lacked native support) and GPT-4o-mini (native tool calling, emails passed as tool messages, instruction-hierarchy trained). Both at top_p 0.92, 1,000-token cap.
datasets_benchmarks: The paper's own output is the benchmark: 208,095 unique attack prompts (169,598 unique across sub-levels) from 839 participants across two phases, with 29,011 auto-labelled as injections because they triggered the send_email API and the rest labelled by an LLM annotator. Four retrieval levels vary mailbox size, retrieval ranking and attacker-email position, with Level 4 additionally requiring exfiltration of a Q2 profit figure.
key_result: Against the full stack of defenses, adaptive human attackers succeeded end-to-end in only 306 of 90,916 phase-2 submissions (0.3%), and some defenses took several hundred attempts before a first success. Ranking by team success rate, LLM Judge was hardest to evade, then TaskTracker, with Prompt Shield the weakest; spotlighting alone beat Prompt Shield, and stacking all defenses improved substantially over any single one. GPT-4o-mini was harder to attack than Phi-3, plausibly from instruction-hierarchy training. Winning strategies clustered on special chat tokens (<|user|>, <|assistant|>, <|end|>), multilingual text, character obfuscation, HTML-like formatting and synthetic conversation blocks that preserve apparent task coherence.
baselines_compared: Four real defenses run as live challenge configurations rather than cited: Spotlighting, Prompt Shield (proprietary black-box classifier), LLM Judge, and TaskTracker (activation-delta linear probe), plus the combination of all, with detection thresholds tuned to under 5% FPR on held-out sets.
threat_model: An external attacker who can only send an email into the victim's mailbox and controls only that email's subject and body. The email must first survive retrieval (in Levels 3-4 it competes on relevance against ten other emails and is inserted statelessly), then evade whatever detection defense is active, then cause the assistant to invoke send_email with exact attacker-specified arguments; Level 4 additionally requires reading a profit figure out of a different email and exfiltrating it. Attackers were adaptive, with unlimited retries and feedback from the challenge interface, but did not know the spotlighting delimiters.
stated_limitations: Authors state Phi-3 was non-deterministic during the competition and had degraded utility under spotlighting, so that configuration was dropped from analysis and phase 2. They note part of the dataset lacks ground-truth labels and relies on an LLM annotator, and that restricting the objective to one specific tool call with fixed arguments limits the diversity of attack goals, so they explicitly advise against training directly on the dataset.
technical_summary: Presents LLMail-Inject, a public adaptive-attack challenge in which 839 participants tried to make a simulated LLM email assistant issue an unauthorized send_email tool call by planting a single email in the victim's mailbox. Crosses four retrieval configurations with four real defenses (Spotlighting, Prompt Shield, LLM Judge, TaskTracker) and their combination, over two backbone models, yielding 208,095 unique attack prompts released as an open benchmark. Analyzes difficulty using a Team Success Rate metric that is robust to teams porting a working attack between sub-levels, and catalogs the strategies that actually defeated each defense. Argues from the data that end-to-end benchmarks and diverse injection styles are what the field is missing, and releases everything as a foundation for structural instruction-data separation work.

rq3.note: Dataset and competition report. It catalogs attacker strategies discovered by participants (special chat tokens, multilingual text, character obfuscation, synthetic conversation blocks) but does not name, formalize or claim any of them as a new technique of its own.

rq4.note: Proposes no defense. It deploys and comparatively stress-tests four existing defenses (Spotlighting, Prompt Shield, LLM Judge, TaskTracker); the contribution is the adaptive-attack dataset and the comparative evaluation.

title: Defense against Prompt Injection Attacks via Mixture of Encodings
artifacts_released: Y - code at https://github.com/ruz048/MoEMEnT
models_evaluated: GPT-4 (turbo-2024-04-09); GPT-4o (2024-05-13); Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct (appendix)
datasets_benchmarks: Safety: BIPIA-derived subset across Email (OpenAI Evals), Table (WikiTableQA), Abstract (XSum) and Code (Stack Overflow), 50 attack types. Helpfulness: 9 NLP datasets - MMLU, Squad, Hellaswag, MGSM, SamSum, WMT, IMDB, WildGuard, WebQ.
key_result: Mixture of encodings (encoding external text under Base64, Caesar and plain in parallel and aggregating the three LLM responses) matches or beats Base64/Caesar alone on attack success rate across all four BIPIA-derived safety datasets for GPT-4 and GPT-4o, while on the helpfulness benchmark it substantially outperforms Base64 and Caesar on math-heavy tasks like MMLU and MGSM and reaches performance close to the no-defense model, avoiding Base64's known utility collapse.
baselines_compared: No Defense, Datamark, Ignoring, Base64, Caesar (Hines et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2024b).
threat_model: Attacker embeds malicious instructions inside external text (documents, tool outputs) that is concatenated with the user prompt and fed to the LLM; the defense is evaluated only against existing static attacks, not an adaptive attacker aware of the mixture-of-encodings scheme.
stated_limitations: Authors state the main limitation is added computational overhead from running the LLM on multiple encoded versions of the prompt in parallel, making it less suitable for time-sensitive applications, though the three calls can be parallelized to mitigate latency.
technical_summary: Proposes mixture of encodings, a prevention-based defense against prompt injection that encodes external text under multiple character encodings (plain, Base64, Caesar cipher) and queries the LLM once per encoding, then aggregates the responses via summed classification probabilities or an LLM meta-prompt for generation tasks. Evaluates on a BIPIA-derived safety benchmark (Email/Table/Abstract/Code) and a 9-task helpfulness benchmark against GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Shows the method keeps the low attack-success-rate of character-encoding defenses like Base64 while avoiding Base64's sharp utility loss on mathematical QA tasks such as MMLU and MGSM.

rq3.note: No attack proposed; purely a prevention-based defense paper.

rq4.name: Mixture of Encodings
rq4.note: Named prevention defense encoding external data under multiple ciphers (Base64+Caesar+plain) and aggregating multi-encoding LLM responses; matches/beats Base64 and Caesar baselines on BIPIA-derived ASR while avoiding Base64's math-task utility loss. Only tested against static (non-adaptive) attacks.

title: ASIDE: Architectural Separation of Instructions and Data in Language Models
artifacts_released: Y - code at https://github.com/egozverev/aside
models_evaluated: Llama 3.1; Llama 2; Qwen 3; Qwen 2.5; Mistral models (multiple sizes each, per model family)
datasets_benchmarks: SEP dataset (9,160 instruction/input pairs, Zverev et al. 2025) for separation scoring; AlpacaEval 1.0 for utility; TensorTrust, Gandalf, Purple, RuLES for direct-attack ASR; BIPIA-text, BIPIA-code, StruQ-ID, StruQ-OOD for indirect-attack ASR.
key_result: Instruction-tuning with ASIDE's fixed 90-degree data-token rotation lowers indirect-injection ASR versus a Vanilla delimiter-based baseline: BIPIA-text 14.7%->4.9%, BIPIA-code 15.3%->8.8%, StruQ-ID 45.6%->28.1%, StruQ-OOD 45%->36% (averages across models), while a competing architectural method (ISE) is within 0.1-2% of Vanilla on the same benchmarks and gives essentially no improvement. Gains come with matched utility and without any dedicated safety training or adversarial examples.
baselines_compared: Vanilla (standard single-embedding architecture) and ISE (Wu et al. 2024, learnable role-offset embeddings).
threat_model: Single-turn (instruction, injection) pairs where token functional role (instruction vs. data) is known at input time by system design (e.g., an email client always labels email contents as data); no adaptive/optimization-based attacker is evaluated, and the setting excludes general chatbots where role must be inferred at runtime.
stated_limitations: Authors state the method is purposefully limited to the single-turn setting where instruction/data roles are well-defined at input time; extending to multi-turn interactions and to role transforms other than rotations, and to multi-tier instruction hierarchies, is left to future work.
technical_summary: Proposes ASIDE, a parameter-free architectural change that applies a fixed orthogonal rotation to the token embeddings of data tokens (while leaving instruction-token embeddings unchanged), giving the model an explicit, learnable-free signal of each token's functional role from the first layer onward. Requires only a modified forward pass plus standard instruction-tuning, with no retraining from scratch and no additional parameters. Evaluated across Llama 3.1/2, Qwen 3/2.5 and Mistral against a Vanilla baseline and the ISE architecture, showing markedly higher instruction-data separation (SEP score) at matched utility and consistently lower attack success rate on both direct (TensorTrust, Gandalf, Purple, RuLES) and indirect (BIPIA, StruQ) prompt-injection benchmarks, without any dedicated safety fine-tuning.

rq3.note: No new attack; a defense/architecture paper only.

rq4.name: ASIDE (Architecturally Separated Instruction-Data Embeddings)
rq4.note: Architectural embedding-level defense (fixed orthogonal rotation on data-token embeddings) requiring only instruction-tuning, not pretraining from scratch; released code; lowers ASR across TensorTrust/Gandalf/Purple/RuLES/BIPIA/StruQ without dedicated safety training. Evaluation is purely adversarial prompt-injection benchmarks, no incidental-degradation testing.

title: Fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs): Improved Prompt Injection Attacks Detection
artifacts_released: N - no code, model or data repository link is given
models_evaluated: XLM-RoBERTa (zero-shot and fine-tuned)
datasets_benchmarks: deepset Prompt Injection Dataset from HuggingFace (546 train / 116 test samples)
key_result: Zero-shot XLM-RoBERTa reaches only 55.17% accuracy (71.67% recall) on the 116-sample test set; after supervised fine-tuning for 50 epochs, accuracy converges to about 99.1% by epoch 10 (100% precision, ~98.3% recall) and plateaus at 98.27% accuracy over the final 10 epochs.
baselines_compared: Zero-shot (non-fine-tuned) XLM-RoBERTa vs. fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa; informally compared in a table against unrelated published accuracies for different tasks/datasets (DistilBERT on Fake-or-Real News, TCNN/TCNN-URG on Weibo) and against a companion paper's multilingual-BERT-plus-classical-classifier result (96.55%) on the same dataset, rather than against any dedicated prompt-injection detector baseline the authors themselves ran.
threat_model: N/A - the task is reduced to offline binary classification of a small, fixed, labeled prompt corpus; no attacker capability, injection channel, or adaptivity is specified.
stated_limitations: No formal limitations section; the abstract only mentions plans to 'analyze incorrect predictions' and the Future Work section says the authors will further fine-tune LLMs. The small 662-sample dataset, absence of adversarial/adaptive evaluation, and the mismatched external comparisons are not acknowledged.
technical_summary: Evaluates zero-shot versus supervised-fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa for binary prompt-injection classification on the small public deepset dataset, tracking accuracy/precision/recall/F1 across 50 fine-tuning epochs. Shows fine-tuning lifts accuracy from 55.17% to roughly 99% within 10 epochs and stabilizes near 98.3% thereafter. A near-identical companion/follow-up study by an overlapping author group (row 1050 in this corpus, c10ab1bf) applies a different embedding+classical-classifier pipeline to the same dataset. Introduces no new architecture, detection principle, or dataset, and performs no adversarial or adaptive evaluation.

rq3.note: No attack or degradation mechanism proposed; purely a binary-classification study.

rq4.note: No named defense. Standard supervised fine-tuning of an existing pretrained encoder (XLM-RoBERTa) on an existing public dataset with its stock split; the pipeline is not named or compared against any actual prompt-injection detector. Same low-value pattern as the companion paper at row 1050 by overlapping authors.

title: UniGuardian: A Unified Defense for Detecting Prompt Injection, Backdoor Attacks and Adversarial Attacks in Large Language Models
artifacts_released: Y - code at https://github.com/huawei-lin/UniGuardian
models_evaluated: Phi 3.5 (3B); Llama 8B; Qwen 32B; Llama 70B
datasets_benchmarks: Prompt Injections; Jailbreak; SST2; Open Question; SMS Spam; Emotion datasets (test splits only); Alpaca 52K (poisoned for backdoor fine-tuning experiments).
key_result: Across prompt injection, fine-tuned backdoor, and adversarial-attack settings, only UniGuardian, LLM-based detection, and Granite-Guardian-3.1-8B meaningfully separate poisoned from clean prompts by auROC/auPRC; Prompt-Guard-86M, PPL detection and Llama-Guard variants perform poorly, especially when the manipulated output is not overtly harmful (e.g. an apology letter rather than toxic content).
baselines_compared: Prompt-Guard-86M; PPL Detection; Llama-Guard-3-1B; Llama-Guard-3-8B; Granite-Guardian-3.1-8B; LLM-based detection; OpenAI Moderation.
threat_model: Attacker either appends prompt-injection instructions to inputs at inference time, or implants a word/phrase trigger via fine-tuning data poisoning to create a dormant backdoor later activated by the trigger; the defender sees only the prompt/input at inference and must classify poisoned vs. clean without knowing which of the three attack families was used.
stated_limitations: Authors state the work focuses only on English-language datasets and large transformer models, so applicability to other languages or architectures is unverified; it is not evaluated on models with very different prompt structures or task-specific fine-tuning; and the suspicious score can still produce false positives or miss subtle, obfuscated backdoor variants.
technical_summary: Proposes UniGuardian, a training-free unified detector for what it terms Prompt Trigger Attacks (PTA) - prompt injection, backdoor, and adversarial attacks. Proves that removing trigger tokens from a poisoned prompt causes a disproportionately larger loss increase than removing non-trigger tokens, then operationalizes this via randomized word-subset removal and z-score analysis of the resulting loss distribution, accelerated by a single-forward strategy that runs concurrently with generation. Evaluates auROC/auPRC across prompt-injection, backdoor, and adversarial-attack settings on 3B-70B models against seven baseline detectors, finding only itself, LLM-based detection and Granite-Guardian meaningfully separate poisoned from clean prompts.

rq3.note: No new attack; defines the umbrella category 'Prompt Trigger Attacks' (PTA) unifying existing prompt injection, backdoor and adversarial attacks conceptually, but proposes no new attack technique.

rq4.name: UniGuardian
rq4.note: Training-free detector using randomized word-removal loss-variance analysis (z-score over masked re-forwarding), accelerated via a single-forward strategy; validated across prompt injection, backdoor and adversarial attacks on 3B-70B models against 7 baselines; released code.

title: LongFaith: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs with Faithful Synthetic Data
artifacts_released: Y - code and datasets at https://github.com/IDEA-FinAI/LongFaith
models_evaluated: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (fine-tuned target); Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct and GPT-4o-mini (used as data-synthesis generators, not defended targets)
datasets_benchmarks: MuSiQue training set (Wikipedia-based multi-hop QA with supporting documents); test sets HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue; LongBench (Qasper, MultiFieldQA-EN, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue variants). Baseline comparison datasets: LongAlpaca, LongAlign, MuSiQue-Attribute, LongMIT, LongReward-SFT/PO, SeaLong-SFT/PO.
key_result: Models fine-tuned on the synthesized LongFaith-SFT and LongFaith-PO datasets outperform models trained on six prior synthetic long-context datasets on most multi-hop reasoning and LongBench test sets, with LongFaith-PO (preference optimization using rejected low-faithfulness samples) consistently beating LongFaith-SFT; some prior synthetic datasets are shown to actually degrade performance below a native, non-fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct baseline.
baselines_compared: Zero-shot Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; models fine-tuned on six prior synthetic long-context datasets (LongAlpaca, LongAlign, MuSiQue-Attribute, LongMIT, LongReward-SFT/PO, SeaLong-SFT/PO), all capped to the same 2K training-sample budget for fairness.
threat_model: N/A - no adversary. 'Knowledge conflicts' here refers to unfaithfulness introduced during synthetic training-data generation (a synthesized reasoning chain citing facts not supported by the provided documents), not an adversarial or incidental context-poisoning scenario encountered at inference time.
stated_limitations: Not explicitly stated as a dedicated limitations section in the excerpted text; the paper frames itself as improving long-context training-data faithfulness and notes ablations on dataset scaling (1K-8K) as an open direction.
technical_summary: Proposes LongFaith, a pipeline for synthesizing faithful long-context reasoning instruction data by grounding synthesized reasoning chains in ground-truth supporting documents via chain-of-citation prompting, and by contrasting these against deliberately unfaithful chains (misinformation, unattributed reasoning, knowledge-conflicting reasoning) to build a preference-optimization dataset (LongFaith-PO) alongside a supervised dataset (LongFaith-SFT). Fine-tunes Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the synthesized data and evaluates on multi-hop QA and LongBench, outperforming six prior synthetic long-context datasets. The 'knowledge conflict' framing concerns faithfulness of synthesized training data relative to source documents during data generation, not an inference-time adversarial or incidental context-poisoning scenario, making this paper tangential rather than central to the corpus's scope.

rq3.note: No adversary and no inference-time degradation mechanism; 'knowledge conflicts' here are training-data faithfulness issues introduced during synthetic data generation, not a context-poisoning phenomenon experienced by a deployed model.

rq4.note: Contributes a training-data synthesis pipeline (SFT + preference-optimization datasets) to improve long-context reasoning faithfulness during fine-tuning, not a runtime defense against poisoned or conflicting context; closer to a dataset/training-method contribution than a deployable ingestion/reasoning/execution intervention against context poisoning.

title: Efficient Universal Goal Hijacking with Semantics-guided Prompt Organization
artifacts_released: N - no repository or code link is mentioned in the text
models_evaluated: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf, Vicuna-7b-v1.5, Guanaco-7B-HF, Mistral-7B-Instruct as victim models
datasets_benchmarks: Training/test prompts sampled from the Alpaca dataset (1,000-sample big pool, 50-sample training subset, 1,000-sample test set); target responses drawn from 10 malicious categories summarized from AdvBench (threatening, bomb, fraud, virus, murder, phishing, financial, drug, racism, suicide); an additional generalization test on the Quora Question Pairs (QQP) dataset.
key_result: POUGH's sampling and ranking strategy for selecting/ordering training prompts, combined with an iterative suffix-optimization algorithm, achieves a universal (cross-prompt) goal-hijacking suffix; ablations show the ASR climbs from 24.7% to 93.0% as the semantic-similarity threshold rises from 0.1 to 0.9, and a naive clustering-based sampling alternative caps ASR at only 77.1% versus the proposed sampling/ranking strategy, demonstrating that prompt selection and ordering (not just the optimization algorithm) materially drives universality.
baselines_compared: Optimization baselines GCG, MAC, AutoDAN, AmpleGCG adapted to universal goal hijacking; handcrafted baselines HouYi and TensorTrust; and M-GCG, described as the only prior optimization method built specifically for universal goal hijacking.
threat_model: White-box attacker with full gradient access to the target LLM who optimizes a single fixed adversarial suffix offline, to be concatenated onto arbitrary future user prompts at inference time to force a targeted harmful response; the attacker does not need real-time optimization, addressing the practicality limitation of prior gradient-based suffix attacks.
stated_limitations: Authors state the prompt-organization strategies (sampling and ranking) likely are not optimal and better semantic-similarity metrics may exist; the study is explicitly restricted to cross-prompt universality and does not address cross-model universality; and testing a 64-token suffix on an A100 could not complete within three days, showing a practical scaling limit.
technical_summary: Proposes POUGH, an optimization-based universal goal-hijacking attack that argues prior work over-focused on the optimization algorithm while neglecting the choice and ordering of training prompts used to fit the adversarial suffix. Introduces a semantics-guided sampling strategy to select a diverse, representative subset of prompts from a candidate pool and a ranking strategy to sequence them, then runs an iterative gradient-based optimization to produce a single suffix that hijacks arbitrary user prompts toward an attacker-chosen malicious response. Evaluated across four open-source 7B models and ten AdvBench-derived malicious-response categories against six attack baselines (GCG, MAC, AutoDAN, AmpleGCG, HouYi, TensorTrust, M-GCG), showing higher attack success rate at lower computational cost than prior universal goal-hijacking methods.

rq3.name: POUGH
rq3.note: Named universal (cross-prompt) goal-hijacking attack combining a semantics-guided prompt sampling/ranking strategy with an efficient gradient-based suffix optimizer; ablations isolate the prompt-organization contribution from the optimization algorithm.

rq4.note: Attack-only paper; proposes no defense and does not evaluate against any existing defense.

title: WalledEval: A Comprehensive Safety Evaluation Toolkit for Large Language Models
artifacts_released: Y - code at https://github.com/walledai/walledeval; datasets at https://hf.co/walledai
models_evaluated: Broad support for open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Gemma families via HuggingFace Transformers) and API-based models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, Together); WalledGuard is compared specifically against LlamaGuard 2.
datasets_benchmarks: 35+ aggregated existing safety benchmarks (e.g. WildJailbreak, JailbreakHub, XSTest) covering multilingual safety, exaggerated safety and prompt injections; introduces two new benchmarks, SGXSTest and HiXSTest, for exaggerated safety in cultural contexts.
key_result: WalledGuard, the toolkit's new small content-moderation classifier, comes within about 3 percentage points of LlamaGuard 2 (the best performer) on XSTest while being smaller and faster; the paper's primary contribution is the aggregation of 35+ existing benchmarks and mutators into one framework rather than a single novel adversarial finding.
baselines_compared: LlamaGuard 2 and other judge/classifier baselines on XSTest for the WalledGuard comparison; the toolkit itself is positioned relative to related frameworks EasyJailbreak and JailbreakEval rather than empirically benchmarked against them.
threat_model: N/A - general-purpose safety-evaluation framework rather than a single threat model; each of the 35+ aggregated benchmarks carries its own attacker assumptions (e.g. jailbreak mutators such as paraphrasing or future-tense rewriting), only one category of which is prompt injection.
stated_limitations: Authors note the framework currently implements only one-to-one text mutators, largely inspired by EasyJailbreak, rather than multi-step attack chains.
technical_summary: Introduces WalledEval, an open-source Python toolkit that aggregates 35+ existing safety benchmarks (spanning multilingual safety, exaggerated safety, prompt injection and jailbreaks) into a unified LLM- and judge-benchmarking framework, with configurable text-mutation attacks for stress-testing. Contributes WalledGuard, a small content-moderation classifier within about 3 points of LlamaGuard 2 on XSTest, plus two new exaggerated-safety datasets, SGXSTest and HiXSTest. Prompt injection is one of many general safety categories the toolkit supports rather than a focal contribution; the paper introduces no new prompt-injection attack or defense technique of its own.

rq3.note: Benchmark/tool paper aggregating existing safety benchmarks and mutators (inspired by EasyJailbreak); introduces no new attack technique of its own.

rq4.note: WalledGuard is a new small content-moderation classifier, but it targets general LLM safety/toxicity judging (benchmarked against LlamaGuard 2 on the exaggerated-safety XSTest dataset), not specifically prompt injection or context poisoning, and is not evaluated against any injection benchmark as a defense.

title: Enhancing Prompt Injection Attacks to LLMs via Poisoning Alignment
artifacts_released: Y - code stated to be publicly available (link given in paper)
models_evaluated: Five prominent LLMs including Llama-3-8b-Instruct (used as the default/best-performing open-source model in main experiments); four open-source LLMs evaluated overall
datasets_benchmarks: Two alignment datasets (ORCA-DPO and a second alignment dataset) used for poisoning; 49 target/injected task pairings drawn from 7 task datasets (MRPC, Jfleg, HSOL, RTE, SST2, SMS Spam, Gigaword) covering duplicate-sentence detection, grammar correction, hate-content detection, NLI, sentiment analysis, spam detection and summarization; MMLU and GPQA used as stealth/capability benchmarks; five distinct prompt injection attacks (including Combined Attack) as the inference-time trigger.
key_result: Poisoning just 10% of the ORCA-DPO alignment data increases the success rate of a Combined prompt-injection Attack against Llama-3-8b-Instruct by an average of 0.33, with observed increases in ASR ranging from 0.17 to 0.33 across configurations; the poisoned models' accuracy on standard capability benchmarks like MMLU stays within 2% of the cleanly aligned model (and is sometimes even better on GPQA), making the poisoning stealthy to routine performance evaluation.
baselines_compared: Clean (unpoisoned) alignment as the control; a conventional backdoor-style poisoning variant (fixed trigger/target response) is compared against PoisonedAlign's prompt-injection-style poisoning, showing the latter is more effective at generally amplifying injection vulnerability; two backdoor/unalignment detectors, BEAT and BAIT, are tested as candidate defenses.
threat_model: A supply-chain attacker who can inject a small fraction (as low as 10%) of poisoned samples into a public or crowdsourced LLM alignment/fine-tuning dataset (e.g. sourced from HuggingFace), without any control over inference-time prompts; the resulting model is then targeted by ordinary inference-time prompt injection attacks, which succeed far more often than against a cleanly aligned model.
stated_limitations: Authors state the poisoning effect is not uniform, varying substantially by base LLM, alignment dataset, and specific target/injected task pairing; and while they tested backdoor-oriented defenses BEAT and BAIT (finding BAIT's Q-SCORE cannot reliably distinguish poisoned from clean alignment because PoisonedAlign does not implant a fixed target response), a comprehensive evaluation against prompt-injection-specific defenses remains for future work.
